title: Finding the right paragraph: keyword search
summary: The oldest way to find the right paragraph is to look for the question's words in your documents and pick the paragraph with the most matches. Search engines make this fast by building an index in advance. It works well, until the question uses a different word.
html:
Lesson 2 ended on a catch: grounding only works if you paste in the right paragraph. So the real question is how you find it, automatically, among thousands of documents. Today is the oldest and simplest answer.

Look for the question's words

Take the words in the question, look for documents that contain them, and pick the one with the most matches. That is it. It is called keyword search, and it is what Ctrl+F does, just across many files at once with a score for each.

A tiny example

Say the whole HR handbook is three paragraphs:

A  "Full time employees receive 24 days of paid leave per year."
B  "Leave requests must be approved by your manager."
C  "The office cafeteria opens at 8 am."

The question is "How many days of leave do I get?" Count how many of the question's words appear in each paragraph:

A  3 matches   days, of, leave
B  1 match     leave
C  0 matches

A wins. Paste A into the prompt, ask the AI, and it answers "24 days". You have just done RAG with no human in the loop: the computer found the paragraph and the AI answered from it.

Little words are noise

Look at why A got its third point: the word "of". That is luck, not meaning. Words like "of", "the", "do" and "I" appear in almost every paragraph, so matching them tells you nothing. They are called stop words, and keyword search either ignores them or gives them almost no weight.

The flip side is that rare words are worth more. "Leave" appears in two of the three paragraphs, so it narrows things down a bit. "Days" appears in only one, so it points straight at A. Real keyword search weighs each word by how rare it is. Lesson 4 and later lessons build on that idea, so it is worth holding onto.

How it stays fast

Reading every document for every question would be slow once you have millions of them. So search engines do the work once, in advance. They build a list: for each word, which paragraphs contain it.

leave     A, B
days      A
manager   B
cafeteria C

Now a search does not read anything. It looks up "days" and "leave" in the list and gets its answer almost instantly. This list is called an index, and it is exactly like the index at the back of a book: you look up a word and it tells you which pages to turn to.

Where it breaks

Ask "How much holiday do I get?" instead. Same meaning. But the word "holiday" is not in paragraph A, and neither is anything else from that question that matters. Every paragraph scores zero. Keyword search finds nothing, even though the answer is sitting right there in A.

That is the big weakness: it matches words, not meaning. Lesson 4 is about exactly that, and it is the reason the rest of the course exists.

New words today

Keyword search: finding documents that contain the words you typed.

Stop words: very common words like "the" and "of" that match everything and so tell you nothing.

Index: a list built in advance of which documents contain which words, so searching does not have to read everything.

All of them are in the glossary.

If you remember one thing
Keyword search finds the paragraph with the most matching words, using an index so it is fast. It works until the question uses a different word for the same thing.

Next lesson: why keyword search misses things, with more examples like "holiday" versus "leave".
exercise:
Run it, five minutes. Paste this into any Python, even an online one, and run it:

paras = {
    "A": "Full time employees receive 24 days of paid leave per year.",
    "B": "Leave requests must be approved by your manager.",
    "C": "The office cafeteria opens at 8 am.",
}
question = "How many days of leave do I get?"

q = set(question.lower().strip("?").split())
for name, text in paras.items():
    words = set(text.lower().strip(".").split())
    print(name, len(q & words))

You should see A 3, B 1, C 0. Now change the question to "How much holiday do I get?" and run it again. Every paragraph scores 0. That is the weakness from the last section, happening in front of you.

Then reply to the email. One line: "done", or the first word that confused you.
